title: A budget trip destroys a worker's in-progress work instead of letting it push what it has
description:
Observed live on run_f7bd5a36c98f44f598cd6cc560b82712 (2026-08-22). Three containers (09w, gm5, 3nh) were dispatched, all booted green, all were working — and all three produced NOTHING. No branch, no report, no salvage. $8.00 spent for zero output.

The wave's own record says why:

  cancelled: {"reason":"budget:cost","detail":"the cost budget is exhausted: $8.00 of $8.00"}
  wait: {"state":"running", ...}
  collect: {"verdict":"no-commits","branch_exists":false}

So the budget tripped, waveCanceller fired, credentials were revoked and the containers were torn down — all correct, and gyl's revoke-before-teardown ordering worked exactly as designed. The problem is what teardown does to work in progress.

TICK 5fg ALREADY SOLVED THIS FOR THE OTHER PATH AND ONLY THAT PATH. When the WORKER's own bound fires, worker.sh salvages uncommitted files into a commit, writes a report and pushes — proven live on run 3, where 5qj's four dirty paths survived as commit adfedff5. But when the SUPERVISOR tears a container down, none of that runs: the container is destroyed with the work inside it. Same loss, different door, and the door 5fg closed is the less likely one.

This is the most expensive failure shape there is, and a budget trip is exactly when it hurts most: the run has by definition just spent its entire allowance, and it then throws away everything that money bought. Run 5 paid $8.00 and kept nothing.

WHAT TO CONSIDER, and the tension is real:
- A cancelled worker needs a bounded grace window to salvage, commit and push before destroy. That window is time a runaway keeps spending — which is precisely what tick gyl argued against for the CREDENTIAL. But the credential is already revoked by then, so a container with no gateway token cannot spend on the model; it can only finish a git push. Revoke-then-grace-then-destroy may give both properties, and that distinction (money dies first, work is rescued second) is the thing to get right.
- The salvage path already exists in worker.sh. The missing piece is a signal from the supervisor that means 'stop and push now' rather than SIGKILL — and confirmation that the container acts on it within the window.
- If a grace window cannot be made safe, the fallback is to make the loss LOUD: the run's report must say that N containers were destroyed mid-work and what it cost, instead of a silent no-commits.

Related, found in the same evidence and worth fixing alongside: the operator asked for --max-cost 40 and got $8, because wrangler.toml's RUN_MAX_COST_USD = "8" clamps it and a submission may only lower a budget. That is the same shape as 5fg's wall-clock clamp — an operator's number silently replaced by a deployment ceiling with no line anywhere saying so. At minimum the submission should REPORT the effective budget it ended up with; `tk cloud run` printed nothing about $8.
acceptance_criteria: A budget trip does not silently destroy in-progress work: either the container is given a bounded post-revocation window to salvage, commit and push (proven live), or the run's outcome states plainly that N workers were destroyed mid-work. And tk cloud run reports the EFFECTIVE cost and wall-clock budget after clamping, so an operator sees the number that will actually apply.
